subject: British History
title: 8. Robert Peel and the Return of the Tories

segments.text: Peel represents nineteenth-century conservatism adapting to a reformed, industrialising society, and the Corn Law crisis is the single key episode for understanding both his significance and his party’s fracture.

blocks.text: Administrative Reform and the Tamworth Manifesto

segments.text: As Home Secretary, Peel reorganised criminal law and helped create the
, emphasising professional administration and public order over purely traditional authority. His

accepted the basic reality of the 1832 Reform Act while promising cautious correction of remaining abuses — a foundational moment in defining a more pragmatic Conservative identity after the collapse of old-style Tory politics.

Peel’s 1841–46 government pursued budget and tariff reform, strengthening state finance while reducing trade barriers in line with growing economic-liberal thinking, and his period also saw factory and mining regulation — showing that Victorian conservatism could accept limited state intervention in social conditions while still defending property and order. In Ireland, Peel placed the Maynooth grant on a more permanent footing and attempted measures to ease tension, but Irish poverty, religious division and land questions remained deeply difficult to resolve.

items.text: Peel’s foundational statement of pragmatic, reform-accepting Conservatism.
Protectionist grain tariffs whose 1846 repeal split the Conservative Party.
Prepare Peel as “old Tory to modern Conservative adaptation”; for every policy, ask whether it reflected pragmatism, economic liberalisation, or social order.
Give special attention to the Irish famine-era context of Corn Law repeal.
Practise one analytical outline answering: “Why did Corn Law repeal split the Conservative Party, and what does this reveal about Peel’s political priorities?”
Do not say Peel was simply a free-market ideologue; he combined economic liberalisation with administrative and social regulation.
Do not separate Corn Law repeal from the Irish famine context and the Anti-Corn Law League campaign.
Do not assume the Conservative Party remained united after 1846.
The Metropolitan Police Act 1829, associated with Peel as Home Secretary, created a professional police force for London.
The Tamworth Manifesto of 1834 is a landmark in the development of modern Conservatism.
Peel served as prime minister in 1834–35 and 1841–46.
The Corn Laws were repealed in 1846, dividing Conservatives between Peelites and protectionists.
Peel illustrates how nineteenth-century conservatism adapted to reform and industrial economics through pragmatic administration rather than fixed ideology.
Corn Law repeal cannot be separated from its Irish famine context, and its consequence — a fractured Conservative Party — matters as much as the policy decision itself.
